issues.legal_issue: A supervisory court is not justified in reappreciating evidence and reversing a concurrent factual finding when the finding is supported by evidence and the lower courts’ proceedings disclose no irrational reasoning, bias, or partiality warranting such intervention.
material_facts: The trial court found that the occupant used the cabin because of his attachment to the hospital as an honorary surgeon, relying on oral and documentary evidence and surrounding circumstances; the appellate court affirmed that finding.

The trial court gave several reasons for refusing a late request to recall a witness and obtain his income-tax returns, including the applicant’s failure to explain the source of newly acquired information and the availability of a prescribed process to seek the information.
The appellate court’s alternative conclusion about whether an assumed licence continued on the relevant date was not necessary to its decision on the actual arrangement between the parties.
The High Court treated those matters as grounds to reappreciate the entire record, although the concurrent factual finding was supported by evidence.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in reappreciating the evidence or reversing the concurrent factual finding, and its judgment could not be sustained.
issues.legal_principle: Article 227 confers supervisory power, not the role of a first appellate court. A concurrent finding of fact supported by evidence cannot be displaced merely because a procedural or evidentiary ruling may be wrong or because an appellate court made an arguably incorrect alternative observation. Unless the reasons given are unreal, flimsy, or irrational so as to disclose a non-judicial approach, bias, or partiality, those matters do not justify a full rehearing of the evidence.

rule.if: supervisory_review_proceeding and concurrent_factual_finding and finding_supported_by_evidence and reasoned_evidence_request_rejection and alternative_observation_inconsequential

predicates.supervisory_review_proceeding: A party asked a supervisory court to review decisions made by lower courts.
predicates.concurrent_factual_finding: Both lower courts reached the same finding on a disputed fact.
predicates.finding_supported_by_evidence: The lower courts’ factual finding had evidence in the record supporting it.
predicates.reasoned_evidence_request_rejection: The trial court rejected a request to obtain further evidence after giving reasons for its decision.
predicates.alternative_observation_inconsequential: The appellate court made an alternative observation that did not affect its decision on the central factual issue.

issues.definition: When a supervisory review concerns a supported factual finding shared by both lower courts, and the cited procedural ruling was reasoned while the alternative observation was inconsequential, the rule means supervisory interference with that finding is not justified.

issues.legal_issue: An occupant who was allowed to use premises because of an attachment to an institution, rather than under a leave-and-licence arrangement, is not entitled to protection as a deemed tenant under the applicable rent-protection provision for licensees.
material_facts: The occupant signed a writing stating that he was attached to the hospital as an honorary surgeon, was allowed to practise privately there, and was neither a tenant nor a licensee; he admitted signing it after understanding its contents.
A witness who had introduced the occupant to the hospital supported the account that use of the cabin was permitted on the same institutional-attachment basis as his own use of another cabin.
A hospital doctor testified that the occupant was consulted on hospital cases in his capacity as an honorary surgeon.
The occupant used the hospital’s operating theatre and related facilities for private patients and received hospital staff services for the cabin and his patients without separate payment.
The receipts produced by the occupant did not state whether the payments were rent, compensation, or contributions to expenses.
The lower courts found that use of the cabin arose from the occupant’s hospital attachment, and the Supreme Court held that the evidence supported that finding.
issues.conclusion: The occupant was not a licensee entitled to protection under section 15A of the Bombay Rent Act as amended by the Maharashtra Act XVII of 1973; his right to use the cabin ended with his hospital attachment.
issues.legal_principle: Section 15A of the Bombay Rent Act, as amended by the Maharashtra Act XVII of 1973, protects qualifying licensees by treating them as tenants. Whether occupation is under a licence depends on the true arrangement shown by the evidence and surrounding circumstances; the label attached to a payment is not conclusive. The Court decided the status issue on the finding that use of the premises arose from institutional attachment, and did not decide the separate questions concerning the statutory definitions of premises or licensee.

rule.if: rent_protection_status_claim and signed_understood_institutional_arrangement and hospital_services_rendered and institutional_facilities_and_staff_provided and corroborating_testimony_supports_attachment

predicates.rent_protection_status_claim: An occupant sought protected-tenant status on the basis that the occupation was licensed.
predicates.signed_understood_institutional_arrangem: The occupant signed and understood a writing recording that use of the premises was allowed because of an attachment to an institution, rather than as a tenant or licensee.
predicates.hospital_services_rendered: The occupant provided professional services to the institution in connection with its work.
predicates.institutional_facilities_and_staff_provi: The institution made its facilities and staff available to the occupant for his work without separate payment.
predicates.corroborating_testimony_supports_attachm: A witness supported the account that the occupant’s use of the premises arose from his institutional attachment.

issues.definition: For a protected-status claim based on licensed occupation, the rule means that when the occupant understood and signed an institutional-attachment arrangement, rendered services, received institutional facilities and staff, and has supporting testimony for that arrangement, the occupant is not protected as a licensee.
